title: Common Core SL.CCR.2 Explained
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart takes the second Speaking and Listening anchor standard - integrate and evaluate information presented in diverse media and formats - and admits it initially baffled him, since it barely mentions speaking and touches listening only in the word 'orally.' Reading the grade 11-12 version, he concludes the standard is really about information overload: students graduate into exponentially increasing amounts of information and must learn to differentiate, evaluate and order it. The move the piece makes is to relocate the standard's purpose from media literacy to decision-making, since the end of all that sorting is making good decisions and solving real problems. Speaking and listening enter because the evaluation is social - students have to talk about masses of information and handle cases where their judgment of a source differs from a peer's. He is comfortable with how loose the standard is, arguing that a teacher who values autonomy should welcome the wiggle room. He then flags a gap: note-taking from non-textual sources such as videos, lectures and discussions appears nowhere in the standards despite being essential. His resolution is that this does not matter, because the CCSS are a framework for equalizing access that was deliberately designed to leave room for locally determined skills.
points: Stuart's reading relocates SL.CCR.2 from a media-formats standard to an information-triage standard whose payoff is better decisions, not better media consumption.
He argues the speaking-and-listening half only makes sense socially: the hard instructional case is two students who evaluate the same source differently and have to talk it through.
He identifies a real curricular gap - note-taking on non-textual sources like video, lecture and discussion is absent from the standards despite being essential for college.
His stance toward vagueness in a standard is that an autonomy-valuing teacher should treat wiggle room as an asset, which is the interpretive posture running through his whole standards series.
He frames the CCSS at their best as an equity instrument - a tool for equalizing access to an education aimed at human flourishing - rather than as a compliance document.
quotes: The 21st century presents the high school graduate with exponentially increasing amounts of information. SL.CCR.2 calls students to the task of dealing with it in collaboration with others.
How do we differentiate and evaluate this information? How do we make order of this info? Most importantly, how do we use this information to make good decisions and solve real problems?
This is the final goal of SL.CCR.2 — using the terabytes of information available to us for the sake of making good decisions. And this is where the speaking and listening come in:
How do we handle situations where my evaluation of an information source differs from a peers? How do we work together to use varied information sources to solve problems that don't seem solvable?

There's lots of wiggle room in SL.CCR.2 and, as a teacher who values autonomy, I am A-okay with that. Speaking of wiggle room, I began working with my freshmen students on note-taking recently, and from what I can tell, taking notes on non-textual sources (e.g., videos, lectures, discussions) isn't explicitly included anywhere in the standards, yet it's obviously croosch for (at least) college and (I would argue) career.

If I'm not, no me importa: remember, the CCSS at their best are a tool for equalizing access to an excellent education designed to promote human flourishing in our current world (i.e., a place where it's pretty baller to know how to read, write, talk, and listen). With that being said, they are just a framework, and they were intentionally designed to leave room for a few locally-determined skills.
